Comprehension:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow.

During much of medieval Europe, monasteries played a crucial role in preserving knowledge at a time when formal education was limited and literacy was rare. Following the decline of the Roman Empire, many centres of learning collapsed, but monastic communities continued to value reading, writing and study as part of their religious life. Monks devoted long hours to copying manuscripts by hand, ensuring the survival of classical texts in philosophy, medicine, history and theology. Monasteries functioned not only as religious institutions but also as intellectual centres. Their libraries became repositories of accumulated knowledge, carefully maintained across generations. In addition to copying ancient works, monks produced commentaries, chronicles and scientific observations, blending classical learning with Christian thought. These activities helped shape medieval scholarship and laid foundations for later intellectual movements. Monastic schools also trained clerics and administrators, indirectly supporting governance and record keeping. Although access to this knowledge remained restricted, the careful preservation of texts meant that Europe did not entirely lose contact with its intellectual past. When universities began to emerge in the later Middle Ages, they drew heavily on materials that monasteries had safeguarded for centuries, making monastic preservation a vital link between antiquity and the Renaissance.
Which activity occupied a large part of monks’ daily work?
